area: Core/Analysis — downstream physics (strain, DPC/iDPC, parallax, ptychography, scientific bundle)
summary: What is genuinely good here: the strain frame question is solved properly. `StrainFrame.swift` derives the scan-frame view live from the calibration, refuses to claim a frame it cannot support (`.detector` with a reason), carries `strain_frame`/`qr_rotation_deg` onto the screen, the burnt caption AND the bundle from one composition site (`ResultExport.swift:445-457`), and I verified its tensor algebra term-for-term against py4DSTEM `latticevectors.py:452-474` and the flip-then-rotate order against `braggvectors.py:538-545` — all correct, including theta as a pseudo-scalar. `tools/strain-frame-test` is a model harness: hand-checkable known answers plus negative controls that plant each specific wrong convention and demand a mismatch. `StrainMapping.compute` matches `get_strain_from_reference_g1g2` exactly, masked positions are NaN not 0 (so a diverging colormap cannot show "no strain"), the w·r² weighting deviation now travels outward as a provenance key, and iDPC's typed refusals and the strain bundle's compute-time origin snapshot are exactly the right shape. The parallax low-order polar decomposition and the aberration gradient basis are faithful ports.  The weakness is asymmetric: everything S7/S8/S13 touched is well-provenanced, and everything they did not — the non-iDPC DPC products, the whole parallax/ptychography family — carries almost nothing. Seven findings; three could change a number, four could make a reader misread one. I re-checked each against `docs/open-items.md` and none of these are already recorded (the DPC "Quantitative" badge at open-items line 1922 is a different, known defect, and I have not re-reported it).

findings.title: DPC angle map holds normalized turns in [0,1) but is stored and displayed as "rad"
findings.why: `DPC.angleImage` deliberately maps atan2 to [0,1) for display (`out[i] = a / twoPi   // [0, 1)`), but `ResultExport.swift:1389` declares the product as `("dpc_angle", "DPC angle", "rad")`. That units string is not decorative: it is rendered beside the result (`UI/ProductWorkspaceViews.swift:497`), burnt into the publication caption (`ResultExport.swift:216`), written into the PNG provenance record as `value_units` (`ResultExport.swift:237`), and written into the sidecar HDF5 alongside the raw float pixels (`ResultExport.swift:729-737`). The pixels are never converted, so the declared unit is wrong by a factor of 2π everywhere the array goes. This is the exact class docs/v2-scope.md §4 exists to refuse — a plausible result a careful user reasonably misreads as a quantitative claim.
findings.failureScenario: User runs DPC on a calibrated dataset, selects the Angle display, and saves the result to the session sidecar. A colleague opens `<file>.mac4dstem.h5`, finds a map named `dpc_angle` with `valueUnits = "rad"` whose values run 0…0.999, and concludes the CoM deflection direction never exceeds ~57° anywhere in the scan. The true range is a full 0…2π turn. Nothing in the file contradicts them.

findings.title: Parallax requires the R–Q transpose, stores it, and then never applies it — `forceTranspose` is hard-coded false and unreachable
findings.why: `ParallaxPhysicalCalibration.resolve` refuses preprocessing outright unless the session has an R–Q rotation (`:47-51`) and captures `transpose: calibration.transposeQR ?? false` (`:89`) and `rotationRad` (`:88`). Neither field is read by any parallax code path — I grepped all six Parallax files plus the two ptychography files; `rotationRad`/`transpose` appear only at their declaration and construction sites. The one place a transpose could enter is `ParallaxLowOrderAberrationOptions.forceTranspose` (`ParallaxAberrationFitting.swift:14`), which defaults to false, and `AppState.fitParallaxAberrations` calls `ParallaxAberrationFitter.fitHigherOrder(preprocessing:alignment:)` with no options argument (`App/AppState.swift:3676-3678`); `grep -rn forceTranspose mac4DSTEM/App mac4DSTEM/UI` returns nothing, so the transposed branch is unreachable from the running app. py4DSTEM threads exactly this value through as `force_transpose` into `_aberration_fit_polar_decomposition` (`References/py4DSTEM-dev/py4DSTEM/process/phase/parallax.py:2274-2310`), where it changes the shift flip, the rotation transpose, and the SIGN of C12a. On a genuinely transposed detector the app's `leastSquaresTransform` gets a matrix with det < 0, the right polar decomposition returns a reflection rather than a rotation (`ParallaxAberrationFitting.swift:523-554` — the comment at :522 acknowledges this branch), and `recovered = -atan2(rotation.m10, rotation.m00)` at :150 is then not a rotation angle at all.
findings.failureScenario: A dataset whose detector axes are transposed relative to the scan — the session's own DPC rotation calibration has already measured `transposeQR = true`, and parallax preprocessing accepted the calibration partly because that field was present. Fit Aberrations runs untransposed: the astigmatism C12a comes out with the wrong sign, and the ContentView panel prints "Fitted rotation: <n>°" (`UI/ContentView.swift:854-860`) for a quantity derived from a reflection matrix. Nothing warns, and the app never compares its own calibrated rotation against the parallax-fitted one.

findings.title: Ptychography rolls every diffraction pattern by one global aperture centre; py4DSTEM rolls each by its own fitted CoM
findings.why: `prepare` re-centres every pattern in the scan with the same scalar shift: `let sourceRow = Float(row) + Float(calibration.originQX)` (:67) and `let sourceColumn = Float(column) + Float(calibration.originQY)` (:73), where those two values are the single session aperture centre captured at `ParallaxPreprocessing.swift:86-87`. py4DSTEM's `_normalize_diffraction_intensities` shifts each pattern by its OWN per-position fitted origin — `shift(diff_intensities[rx, ry], (-com_fitted_x[rx, ry], -com_fitted_y[rx, ry]), mode="grid-wrap")` (`References/py4DSTEM-dev/py4DSTEM/process/phase/phase_base_class.py:1442-1457`) — which is how descan is removed before the reconstruction. This is a py4DSTEM port deviation with no inline `DEVIATION` note, violating the repo hard rule, and it is not a limitation of the app's data: the per-position maps already exist as `calibration.origin.fittedX/fittedY` and are read a few hundred lines away in `Support/ResultExport.swift:1347-1357`. The exported ptychography provenance (`ResultExport.swift:1664-1680`) records engine, method, iterations, step size and eight constraint flags but says nothing about which origin was used or that descan was not removed, so the omission is invisible downstream.
findings.failureScenario: A scan with ordinary descan — the beam centre drifting a few detector pixels across the scan, which is precisely why `OriginCalibration.fitOrigin` exists. Every pattern is rolled by the mean origin, so each position's amplitude array carries a position-dependent centring error. The single-slice engine has no way to attribute that to descan and absorbs it as object and probe phase, producing a smoothly varying phase ramp across the reconstruction that reads as real specimen structure. The exported `ptychography_object_phase` map is in "rad" with full engine provenance and no hint the input was mis-centred.

findings.title: Every non-iDPC DPC product exports with `analysis_mode` as its only provenance key — no rotation, no transpose, no mrad scale
findings.why: `currentScalarPersistenceMetadata` gates its rich DPC branch on `analysisMode == .dpc, dpcDisplay == .idpc` (:1477). Magnitude, magnitude-in-mrad, angle and colour-wheel miss that branch, miss strain (:1525), acom (:1561) and disks (:1582), and land on the fall-through at :1593-1597, which returns `["analysis_mode": analysisMode.rawValue]` — one key. Two consequences are load-bearing. (a) The DPC angle is frame-dependent: `AppState.applyDPCDisplay` rotates the CoM field by the calibrated R–Q angle and transpose before building the image (`App/AppState.swift:4380-4383`, then :4402), so the exported angle map is meaningless without the angle that was applied — and that angle is recorded nowhere in the file. (b) `dpc_magnitude_mrad` declares units "mrad" (:1388) from a conversion that depends on the accelerating voltage and the Q pixel size (`App/AppState.swift:4440-4454`); neither the mrad-per-pixel factor nor its two inputs appear in the record. Contrast the iDPC branch immediately above, which carries seven keys including `reciprocal_angstrom_per_detector_pixel` and a `qualitative_reason` — the asymmetry shows this is an omission, not a decision.
findings.failureScenario: User calibrates the R–Q rotation to 37°, exports the DPC angle map as a publication PNG, then next session re-runs rotation calibration on a re-cropped view and gets 128°. The two exported figures show completely different angle fields for the same specimen and neither PNG's metadata record contains a rotation, a transpose, or an origin — there is no way to tell which is which, or to reproduce either.

findings.title: Parallax corrected phase and depth sections export none of the aberration coefficients that define them
findings.why: `parallax_corrected_phase` provenance is exactly four keys — source_product, full_fit, q_lowpass, q_highpass (:1624-1629) — and `parallax_depth` is five, adding depth_angstrom, information limit and power (:1638-1644). But the corrected phase IS the aligned BF image multiplied by a transfer function built entirely from `fit.terms` and `fit.coefficientsAngstrom` (`Core/Analysis/ParallaxAberrationCorrection.swift:98-133`), and the depth stack's CTF is built from the same coefficients (`Core/Analysis/ParallaxDepthSectioning.swift:126-148`), with `chi = pi * wavelength * fit.lowOrder.c1Angstrom * frequency2` in the non-full-fit branch (:147). None of C1, C12a, C12b, the fitted rotation, the term list, the fit method or the shift-fit RMS reaches the exported record. They are shown on screen (`UI/ContentView.swift:852-909`) and then dropped at export. `depth_angstrom` is especially exposed: depth is measured from the fitted defocus reference plane, and that reference is the unrecorded C1.
findings.failureScenario: A user exports `parallax_depth` at "depth_angstrom = 64", then re-fits aberrations with `fitMethod = .global` instead of the default `.recursive` (a supported option, `ParallaxAberrationFitting.swift:50`) and exports again at the same nominal 64 Å. The two images are of different physical planes because C1 changed, but the two files' provenance dictionaries are byte-identical. Nothing in either file distinguishes them.

findings.title: Higher-order aberration gradient basis is sampled at BF-centroid angles, not py4DSTEM's array-centre angles — and the parity harness re-implements the app's convention so it cannot see the difference
findings.why: `gradientSamples` iterates `for angle in probeAnglesMrad` (:344) and takes u,v straight from those angles (:345-350). Those angles are built centroid-relative: `meanQX/meanQY` are the mean of the selected bright-field indices, and `reciprocalVectors` subtract them (`ParallaxPreprocessing.swift:260-269`), which correctly matches py4DSTEM's `_kxy` (`parallax.py:473-477`) — but `_kxy` is only used for the LOW-order fit. For the higher-order basis py4DSTEM builds the grid with `sampling = 1/(reciprocal_sampling * region_of_interest_shape)` (`parallax.py:2444-2446`) into `fftfreq(nx, sx)` (`utils.py:1551-1553`) and then samples it at `corner_indices = self._xy_inds - roi_shape // 2` (`parallax.py:2460-2463`) — i.e. at angles relative to the DETECTOR ARRAY CENTRE, not the disk centroid. When the BF disk is not centred on the detector the two bases differ by a constant angular offset, which changes every fitted coefficient of radial order ≥ 2. The parity harness cannot catch this: `tools/parallax-aberration-test/reference.py:140-146` recomputes u,v directly from the same `angles` array the app uses, so it pins the app against a hand-written model that already assumes the app's centring — a green test that agrees with the code by construction. Its source-lock contracts (`reference.py:37-45`) check the formula strings in `utils.py` but not the grid the formula is evaluated on.
findings.failureScenario: A dataset where the beam sits ~15 detector pixels off the array centre (routine). The app fits C21/C23 coma and trefoil against a basis offset in angle from py4DSTEM's; the coefficients disagree with a py4DSTEM run on the same file, and `run-tests.sh scientific` stays green because the harness shares the app's assumption. Which convention is physically right is arguable — py4DSTEM is internally inconsistent here — but the app silently picks the other one with no `DEVIATION` note, violating the repo hard rule.

findings.title: Strain local fit residual uses a weighted RMS where py4DSTEM uses a weighted mean; the existing DEVIATION note covers only the fit weighting
findings.why: `fitLattice` returns `residual: Float(sqrt(squaredResidual / weightSum))` accumulating `weight * (dx*dx + dy*dy)` (:612-628) — a weighted RMS of the per-peak Euclidean distance. py4DSTEM's `fit_lattice_vectors` computes the per-peak distance and then `error = np.sum(error * weights) / np.sum(weights)` (`References/py4DSTEM-dev/py4DSTEM/process/strain/latticevectors.py:215-216`) — a weighted MEAN. By Jensen these differ, always in the same direction (RMS ≥ mean), and the gap grows with residual spread. The `DEVIATION` block at StrainMapping.swift:585-592 is careful and well-measured but is explicitly about the fit's Σw·r² vs Σw²·r² weighting; it says nothing about the residual statistic. That number is not internal: it is exported as the `strain_fit_residual` field in "detector_px" (`Support/ResultExport.swift:512-513`) and as `local_residual_median_pixels` in the displayed-result provenance (`ResultExport.swift:1538-1540`), and it is offered as a selectable display component (`StrainComponent.residual`).
findings.failureScenario: A colleague validating the app against py4DSTEM on the same Bragg vectors compares the exported `strain_fit_residual` map to py4DSTEM's `g1g2_map['error']` slice. On a position with a spread of peak residuals the app reads systematically higher — enough to look like a real fit-quality regression — and the one DEVIATION note in the file points at a different quantity, so the reader concludes the fit itself is worse rather than that a different statistic is being reported.
